A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeLutra. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark experiments, ablations, error analyses, and appendix code-quality assessment results.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds self-debugging and GPT-4 preference comparisons in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The execution-based classification of generated code, preference-pair sampling, iterative refinement, and combined DPO/SFT objective remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. The Bradley–Terry discussion explains the existing approach rather than introducing a component.

E1.justification: Both versions use Spider and BIRD for SQL generation and DS-1000 for Python data-science tasks, with the retained BIRD code-assessment analysis. The new comparisons use existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds SFT + Self-debug as a Spider comparator in Table 6 and GPT-4-generated preferences as a DS-1000 comparator in Table 7. The main benchmark comparator set and earlier DPO/SFT comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new appendix experiments introduce self-debugging and GPT-4-based preference labeling as experimental controls. Existing splits, metrics, 16-response collection, and four one-epoch refinement iterations are retained. Newly specified decoding settings for existing evaluations are disclosures rather than demonstrated protocol revisions.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds a targeted test of preference-source choice, comparing GPT-4 judgments with execution results. Earlier negative-sample, data-volume, loss, ground-truth, backbone, and error analyses remain. The relocated SQL example and code-assessment table are retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new tables retain that reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Table 6 reports Spider execution accuracy of 69.2% for SFT + Self-debug, versus 67.9% for SFT and 76.3% for CodeLutra. Table 7 reports DS-1000 accuracy of 27.8% with GPT-4 preferences versus 48.2% with execution preferences. Existing results remain unchanged; 76.3% and 48.2% already appear in Table 1's fourth-iteration row.

T1.justification: The loss and full mathematical specification in Algorithm 1 remain equivalent. Standard preliminary notation is shortened or replaced with prose, without substantive changes to definitions, assumptions, or reasoning. No theorem or proof is added or removed.

C1.justification: The central claims remain data-efficient iterative learning from successful and failed generations, improved smaller-model performance approaching or exceeding GPT-4 on the reported tasks, and the importance of negative examples and likelihood regularization. Rewriting preserves the main contribution statements and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds a hypothesis that GPT-4 preferences underperform because of weak execution grounding and heuristic judgments, plus an ethics discussion identifying possible amplification of errors through self-generated data. Appendix A expands mechanism explanations and uses broader ground-truth-free language. The original correctness-only and undifferentiated-error limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.6 newly specifies evaluation temperature 0.2, top-p 1.0, a 512-token limit, and SFT baseline training settings. Table 2 now identifies DPO as fine-tuned from an SFT model, and B.2 states approximate preference-data totals. These clarify documentation without establishing reruns; the original hyperparameter table is retained.

R1.justification: The rewritten related work and new Appendix A substantially refocus positioning around execution-feedback methods and iterative preference learning. V2 adds discussion of CodeRL, NExT, RLAIF, and Liu et al.'s dual-loss theory, explicitly acknowledging prior theoretical foundations while expanding methodological contrasts. Numerous broader citations from v1 are removed.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites and condenses the abstract, introduction, preliminaries, method explanations, and related work. Related work moves from Section 6 to Section 2; task and dataset descriptions move into the appendix; the takeaway box is removed; and the supplement is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The document changes from one-column to two-column layout, substantially altering text flow and figure/table placement. Two comparison tables are added, and v1's main-text Figure 5 moves to appendix Figure 7. Existing plots are retained, while tables and examples are repositioned and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful methodological controls in Tables 6–7 and improves reproducibility through Appendix B.6's decoding and baseline settings, while retaining the original results. Its expanded literature discussion also acknowledges prior dual-loss foundations. The net gain is limited: the new controls remain briefly specified, and Appendix A's broad ground-truth-free wording is difficult to reconcile with Algorithm 1's reference-based verification.
